concept.name: Average directional index
concept.definition: Welles Wilder's trend-strength gauge (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978): the Wilder-smoothed average of the Directional Movement Index (DX), which measures the spread between +DI and -DI relative to their sum; ADX quantifies trend strength on a 0-100 scale regardless of direction.
concept.intuition: ADX answers 'is the market trending at all?', not which way - Wilder suggested readings above 25 indicate a strong trend and below 20 the absence of one.
concept.mechanics: Compute +DM, -DM and True Range, smooth each with Wilder's technique over 14 periods, derive +DI and -DI, then DX = 100 x |+DI - -DI| / (+DI + -DI); ADX is the 14-period Wilder-smoothed average of DX. Roughly 150 periods of data are needed for stable values.
concept.formula: DX = 100 x |+DI14 - -DI14| / (+DI14 + -DI14); first ADX = 14-period average of DX, then ADX_t = ((ADX_{t-1} x 13) + DX_t) / 14.
concept.failure_modes: Heavy double smoothing makes ADX very laggy - it often confirms a trend only near its end; it cannot distinguish up from down, and in flat markets it offers no usable signal.
concept.misconceptions: A rising ADX does not mean prices are rising - ADX also rises in strong downtrends; and a falling ADX means the trend is weakening, not that it has reversed.
concept.example: If +DI = 32 and -DI = 12, DX = 100 x 20/44 ~ 45.5; sustained DX values near this level push ADX above 25, Wilder's strong-trend threshold.
